kaigo-atomic-skeleton-functions.heading: Five bone functions and the spine
paragraphs: Bones support body shape and provide a foundation for movement together with muscles and joints. Bones of many sizes connect to form the skeleton and support the body even when not walking.

The skull, ribs and other bones protect internal organs. Bones also store calcium, and bone marrow contributes to blood-cell production. Distinguish support, movement, protection, storage and blood formation.

The spine has physiological curves and is described as S-shaped when viewed from the side. Its appearance alone does not allow you to diagnose a spinal disease. Clearly communicate the posture, pain or other conditions that you have actually confirmed.
[Learning comparison] Saying bones exist only for walking omits organ protection, blood formation and calcium storage. These functions still matter for people needing walking assistance.

This section explains how the body works. The actual method of assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan and practical training. Do not use this explanation alone as a basis for correcting someone’s posture or starting exercise.

kaigo-atomic-skeleton-labels.heading: Bone names, fracture sites and osteoporosis
paragraphs: The skull is in the head; the sternum and ribs are in the chest. The spine consists of connected vertebrae, with regional names including cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. Distinguish specific bones from broad areas such as chest and lower back.

The humerus is in the upper arm; the radius and ulna are in the forearm. The thigh contains the femur, whose neck is one part near the hip. Distinguish the two forearm bones from the thigh bone and check their locations.

The textbook lists the humerus, radius, spine and femoral neck as common fracture sites in older adults. Learning site names differs from diagnosing a fracture from pain. Do not independently replace the precise recorded or illustrated location with a broader term.

Osteoporosis reduces bone strength and increases fracture risk. Prolonged inactivity, nutrition and hormonal changes can contribute. Risk may rise after menopause, but men can also develop it. Do not decide an individual’s condition from age or sex alone.

A curved back, reduced height and back pain can inform assessment but do not establish osteoporosis alone. Check individual needs and safety when supporting calcium-containing meals, activity or opportunities for sunlight. Fall-preventive surroundings also matter.

[Learning comparison] If a record identifies the femoral neck, reporting only ‘thigh’ loses necessary precision. Communicate the confirmed site and the person’s own words without adding unassessed fractures or disease names.

kaigo-atomic-muscle-labels.heading: Read muscle locations from front and back
paragraphs: The deltoid is around the shoulder, and the pectoralis major is at the front of the chest. In the upper arm, identify the biceps brachii at the front and the triceps brachii at the back. Before reading a muscle diagram, first check whether it shows the front or the back of the body.

Learn the iliopsoas involved in hip movement, gluteus maximus in the buttocks, quadriceps femoris at the front thigh and biceps femoris at the back thigh with their locations. ‘Biceps’ alone does not identify upper arm or thigh; retain the needed regional name.
Muscles contribute to movement and posture. They are also part of internal-organ structures, not only limbs. Beyond separate bone, joint and muscle names, consider their cooperation during actions.

[Learning check] Biceps brachii and biceps femoris are different muscles. Shared name elements do not remove the need to check location and diagram orientation. Knowing a name does not determine a person’s training load or exercises.

kaigo-atomic-senses.heading: How sensory stimuli reach the brain
paragraphs: Besides receiving light through eyes and sound through ears, senses include smell, taste and touch. Sensory-organ stimuli travel through nerves to the brain for processing.

The transparent lens helps focus light. The retina at the back of the eye receives light stimuli; information travels through the optic nerve to the brain. Lens, retina and optic nerve do not have identical functions.

The lens has two outward-curving surfaces. Do not read cross-section curves as a separate sphere inside the eye. The retina is membrane-like tissue across the back of the eye. Connect diagram shapes with actual positions and roles.

The eardrum receives sound vibrations, which the ossicles amplify and transmit to the inner ear. Sensory cells in the cochlear duct and related structures convert vibrations to signals that travel along the auditory nerve to cerebral hearing areas. Distinguish mechanical vibration transmission from neural signals.

[Learning comparison] A person’s improved ability to understand sounds while using a hearing aid does not establish that their entire auditory pathway is normal. Check which communication methods they can understand and what they prefer. Consult the appropriate professionals about any necessary assessment or adjustment of the device.

kaigo-atomic-circulation.heading: Four heart chambers and two circulations
paragraphs: The heart has four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle. Atria receive returning blood; ventricles pump it out. Right and left are not independent hearts but work within connected circulation. Heart muscle repeatedly contracts to eject blood and relaxes to receive it.

Blood returns from the body through the superior and inferior vena cava to the right atrium, then travels from the right ventricle through pulmonary arteries to the lungs. After oxygen and carbon-dioxide exchange, pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium. This is pulmonary circulation.

Blood passes from left atrium to left ventricle and through the aorta and its branches to the body. After exchange with tissues, veins return it to the right atrium; this is systemic circulation. The superior vena cava mainly collects blood from upper regions, the inferior from lower regions.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and pulmonary veins oxygen-rich blood, so ‘arteries always contain more oxygen’ is incorrect. Fine capillaries participate in exchange with tissues.

Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, waste and other materials. Lymph also relates to fluid movement and immunity. Circulation explanations teach routes and functions, not judgments about actual blood or disease from diagram colors alone.

kaigo-atomic-digestive.heading: Digestive route and bowel-movement mechanisms
paragraphs: Food passes from mouth through esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Stomach movement and digestive juices aid digestion; the small intestine absorbs nutrients and water. The large intestine also absorbs water and forms stool.

The digestive system includes the tract from mouth to anus and organs producing digestive fluids and related substances. Breakdown and absorption differ from passing remaining material as stool. The large intestine does not replace all major nutrient absorption in the small intestine.

Large-intestine regions include ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon. Stool filling the rectum stimulates its wall and contributes to the urge for a bowel movement. Anal sphincters and other structures coordinate stool passage.

Excretion includes urine, sweat and carbon dioxide leaving through their respective routes, not only stool. Observations provide health clues, but assistance follows checks of which action the person finds difficult.
The urge may weaken while waiting. Saying ‘I no longer want to go’ does not establish an empty rectum. Listen to habits and concerns and support timely toileting according to the plan.

The textbook gives leaning forward and raising heels as an example of a posture easing bowel movements. It illustrates posture’s relationship with the rectum-to-anus passage. Prioritize individual foot support, balance and assessed posture rather than asking someone to strain or force weak legs to raise the heels.

[Learning comparison] Difficulty reaching the toilet in time calls for checks of sensation, finding the place, the route, clothing and waiting for help. Do not diagnose excretory-organ disease from the outcome alone; support needed actions.

kaigo-atomic-endocrine.heading: Distinguish endocrine-gland locations and roles
paragraphs: Endocrine glands secrete hormones into blood to regulate bodily functions. Gland names differ from hormone names and from tubes carrying urine.

Identify the pituitary and pineal glands in the head and thyroid and parathyroid glands in the neck. The thymus is in the chest and adrenal glands above the kidneys. Nearby organs do not necessarily share functions.

The pancreas secretes hormones involved in blood-glucose regulation. Ovaries and testes appear as gonads too. The location list covers nine names: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas, ovaries and testes.

[Learning comparison] Adrenal endocrine function differs from urine production in the kidneys. Similar names or locations do not establish identical functions. Do not use this lesson to diagnose hormonal abnormalities or change medication or food.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-skeleton-functi.prompt: What is missing from the statement that bones exist only for walking?
options: An explanation that bones have no function in someone who does not walk.
Support, organ protection, calcium storage and blood formation.
An explanation that all bones are the same size.
A method of diagnosing disease from spinal shape alone.
rationales: Bones provide support and protection even when the person is not walking.
Movement alone does not explain their multiple roles; include support, protection, storage and blood formation.
Bones vary in size, so an identical-size explanation is incorrect.
The task is to add missing functions, not a shape-only diagnostic method.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-skeleton-labels.prompt: A recorded diagram identifies the femoral neck. How should its location be reported?
options: Specify the confirmed femoral neck and do not conclude fracture from pain alone.
‘Thigh’ always means exactly the same location.
Femoral neck is another name for a forearm bone.
Record fracture from pain without further checking.
rationales: Preserve the precise location and distinguish it from an unassessed diagnosis.
The femoral neck is one part, not the whole thigh.
The forearm contains radius and ulna; the femoral neck is near the hip.
Pain matters, but alone does not diagnose a fracture.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-muscle-labels.prompt: Which explanation of biceps brachii and biceps femoris is correct?
options: Shared name elements mean the same muscle.
Both occur only on the front chest.
They are separate upper-arm and thigh muscles; check region and front/back view.
Knowing muscle names permits independently choosing exercise loads.
rationales: Shared words do not make muscles in different regions identical.
One is in the upper arm and the other the thigh, distinct from chest muscles.
This preserves location and checks diagram orientation.
Exercise loads require checking condition and plan, beyond terminology alone.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-senses.prompt: What can be concluded when a hearing aid improves sound understanding?
options: The whole hearing pathway is confirmed normal.
Improvement is known, but the entire pathway is not confirmed normal; check suitable communication.
Eardrum and ossicles are no longer needed.
Omit personal hearing checks and use identical settings for everyone.
rationales: A response to one aid cannot assess every stage of the pathway.
This separates observed improvement from the unconfirmed whole-pathway assessment.
Hearing-aid use does not make bodily hearing functions unnecessary.
Hearing varies; check personal responses and wishes.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-circulation.prompt: Why is ‘all arteries carry oxygen-rich blood’ incorrect?
options: Arteries always return to the heart.
Pulmonary veins contain no oxygen.
Red diagram color alone defines an artery.
Arteries leave the heart; pulmonary arteries carry blood before lung gas exchange.
rationales: Veins are defined by return toward the heart.
Pulmonary veins return blood oxygenated in the lungs to the left atrium.
Color is an illustration choice, not the vessel definition.
Names follow heart-relative direction, making pulmonary arteries an exception to oxygen-based generalization.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-digestive.prompt: Why does failing to reach the toilet in time alone not establish excretory-organ disease?
options: Movement and clothing have no role in toileting.
An urge always guarantees independent timely access.
Sensation, finding the place, mobility, clothing and support timing all contribute.
The person’s concern about not arriving can never be recorded.
rationales: Toileting includes reaching the place and handling clothing.
Even with an urge, other conditions such as movement may prevent timely access.
Check the difficult stage rather than replacing one outcome with an organ-disease diagnosis.
Record the person’s concern separately from observations and unknown conditions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-endocrine.prompt: Which explanation distinguishes adrenal glands from kidneys?
options: Adrenals are endocrine glands; kidneys produce urine. Nearby location does not mean identical function.
Adrenal gland is another name for ureter.
Adrenal and kidney are two names for one organ.
Adrenal gland is the tube draining urine from the bladder.
rationales: This distinguishes endocrine function from urine production despite similar names and locations.
The ureter carries urine from kidney to bladder and differs from the adrenal gland.
These are separate organs, not alternative names.
The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body; this is not the adrenal gland.
